title: Promises
summary: A **Promise** is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It is always in one of three states — **pending**, **fulfilled**, or **rejected** — and lets you attach `.then`/`.catch`/`.finally` handlers to run code when the result is ready, replacing nested callbacks with flat, composable chains.

subtopics.title: The three states
subtopics.explanation: A promise starts pending (the async work hasn't finished). It then settles exactly once, becoming either fulfilled (resolved with a value) or rejected (failed with a reason). Once settled, a promise is immutable — its state and value never change again, which makes promises safe to pass around and attach handlers to even after they've settled.

subtopics.title: then / catch / finally
subtopics.explanation: .then(onFulfilled, onRejected) registers handlers for the settled value. .catch(onRejected) is shorthand for .then(undefined, onRejected) and handles rejections. .finally(fn) runs regardless of outcome (cleanup) and passes the value/reason through unchanged. Each of these returns a NEW promise, which is what enables chaining.

subtopics.title: Chaining and value transformation
subtopics.explanation: Because every .then returns a new promise, you can chain steps top-to-bottom. Whatever a .then callback returns becomes the fulfillment value of the next .then. Crucially, if a callback returns a promise, the chain WAITS for it to settle and unwraps its value before continuing — this is how you sequence dependent async steps without nesting.

subtopics.title: Combinators: all, allSettled, race, any
subtopics.explanation: Promise.all(arr) waits for all to fulfill (or rejects on the first rejection) and returns an array of values. Promise.allSettled(arr) waits for all to settle and returns {status, value/reason} for each, never rejecting. Promise.race(arr) settles as soon as the FIRST promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). Promise.any(arr) fulfills with the first FULFILLMENT, rejecting only if all reject (with an AggregateError).
subtopics.example: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]); // parallel

subtopics.title: Error propagation
subtopics.explanation: A rejection (or a thrown error inside a .then callback) skips all subsequent .then handlers and jumps to the next .catch in the chain — like throw/catch but for async. One .catch at the end can therefore handle errors from any earlier step. After a .catch handles the error, the chain returns to the fulfilled track unless the handler re-throws.

subtopics.title: Creating a promise
subtopics.explanation: new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }) wraps a callback-based or timed operation. The executor runs synchronously; you call resolve(value) on success or reject(reason) on failure. Promise.resolve(v) and Promise.reject(e) create already-settled promises. This is how you 'promisify' legacy callback APIs.
subtopics.example: const wait = ms => new Promise(res => setTimeout(res, ms));

subtopics.title: Microtask timing
subtopics.explanation: Promise reaction callbacks (.then/.catch/.finally) always run as MICROTASKS — on the same tick, after the current synchronous code finishes but before any setTimeout/macrotask. So even a Promise.resolve().then(...) runs after all sync code, yet before a setTimeout(0) scheduled earlier. This ordering is a frequent interview question.

foundations.overview: Promises are JavaScript's standard abstraction for asynchronous results. Instead of passing a callback to be invoked later, an async function returns a promise object you can attach handlers to. Promises solved callback hell by enabling flat chaining, gave async code real error propagation, and provided combinators for coordinating multiple operations. They are also the foundation async/await is built on.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion (fulfillment) or failure (rejection) of an asynchronous operation, holding a state (pending/fulfilled/rejected) and, once settled, an immutable value or reason, with .then/.catch/.finally methods to register reaction callbacks that run as microtasks.
foundations.whyItMatters: Nearly all modern async APIs (fetch, IndexedDB wrappers, many libraries) return promises, and async/await is just syntax over them. Understanding states, chaining, error propagation, combinators, and microtask timing is essential for correct, readable async code and is heavily tested in interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a promise as a claim ticket from a coffee shop: you don't get the coffee immediately (pending), but you hold a ticket you can act on. Eventually it's ready (fulfilled) or they're out of beans (rejected). You pre-arrange what to do in each case with .then and .catch.
foundations.browserPerspective: The async work (e.g., a network request) runs via host Web APIs off the main thread. When it settles, the engine schedules the promise's reaction callbacks on the MICROTASK queue, so they run right after the current synchronous code and before any timer callbacks.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Data fetching with fetch().then(...), running independent requests in parallel with Promise.all, racing a request against a timeout with Promise.race, resilient batch loads with Promise.allSettled, and promisifying legacy callback APIs.
foundations.businessImpact: Promises make async flows readable and reliable, reducing bugs and speeding development; combinators like Promise.all cut latency by parallelizing requests, directly improving load times and user experience.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Promises give async code structured error handling and composability; understanding them is prerequisite to async/await and to reasoning about execution order via the microtask queue.
foundations.performanceImpact: Running independent work in parallel with Promise.all instead of awaiting sequentially dramatically reduces total latency. Reaction callbacks are microtasks, so heavy promise chains can still block rendering if they never yield to macrotasks.
commonUseCases: Fetching data and transforming it through a .then chain
Parallelizing independent requests with Promise.all / allSettled
Racing an operation against a timeout with Promise.race
Promisifying callback-based APIs with new Promise(...)

commonMisconceptions.myth: A promise can resolve and then later reject (or change value).
commonMisconceptions.reality: A promise settles exactly once and is then immutable; further resolve/reject calls are ignored.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Promise.all runs the promises — it starts them in parallel.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The promises are already running when you pass them; Promise.all just waits for all of them and aggregates results (rejecting on the first failure).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A .then callback runs immediately when the promise resolves.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It runs as a microtask after the current synchronous code finishes — so it's deferred to the end of the current tick, before any setTimeout.

visualExplorer.title: Promise reactions run as microtasks
visualExplorer.caption: See why a .then callback runs after synchronous code but before a setTimeout(0) macrotask.

config.intro: Trace a snippet that logs synchronously, schedules a setTimeout, and resolves a promise.

steps.name: Run synchronous logs
steps.detail: Top-level console.log statements execute first on the call stack.

steps.name: Schedule the timer
steps.detail: setTimeout(0) queues its callback on the macrotask (task) queue.

steps.name: Resolve the promise
steps.detail: Promise.resolve().then(...) queues its reaction on the microtask queue.

steps.name: Stack empties
steps.detail: All synchronous code finishes; the call stack is empty.

steps.name: Drain microtasks
steps.detail: The .then reaction runs now — before the timer — because microtasks drain first.

steps.name: Run the macrotask
steps.detail: Only afterward does the setTimeout callback run on the next tick.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: fulfilled: done, then cleanup runs always.

codeLab.title: Promisify a callback API
codeLab.instructions: Implement delay(ms) that returns a promise resolving after ms, and promisify(fn) that turns an error-first callback function into one that returns a promise. Resolve with the result, reject with the error.
hints: delay just wraps setTimeout in new Promise and calls resolve.
promisify returns a function that appends an error-first callback which resolves or rejects.

debuggingLab.title: A broken chain that swallows the result
debuggingLab.symptom: The final .then logs undefined instead of the transformed value.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The first .then callback computes n * 2 but doesn't RETURN it, so the callback returns undefined. Whatever a .then returns becomes the next .then's input — so the next handler receives undefined. A missing return is the most common promise-chain bug.
commonMistakes: Assuming the last expression in a .then is auto-returned (it isn't with a block body).
Not returning a value/promise from a .then, breaking the chain's data flow.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Return the computed value (or use a concise arrow body) so it flows to the next .then.

theory.question: What are the three states of a promise, and what does it mean for a promise to be settled?
theory.directAnswer: A promise is pending (not yet done), fulfilled (completed with a value), or rejected (failed with a reason). 'Settled' means it has moved out of pending into either fulfilled or rejected — and crucially this happens exactly once and is then immutable, so its state and value can never change again.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A finite state model for the lifecycle of an async result.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It gives async operations a predictable, one-way lifecycle so handlers can attach safely and run at most once.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Creation puts it in pending; calling resolve transitions to fulfilled, reject to rejected; subsequent settle calls are ignored.

theory.whyImportant: Immutability and single-settlement are what make promises safe to pass around and chain; it's foundational interview knowledge.
theory.realWorldExample: fetch() returns a pending promise that becomes fulfilled with a Response or rejected on a network error.

nestedTopics.title: Immutability
nestedTopics.explanation: Once settled, value and state are fixed.

nestedTopics.title: Attach after settle
nestedTopics.explanation: Handlers added to an already-settled promise still run (as microtasks).

followUps.question: Can a promise go from fulfilled back to pending?
followUps.answer: No — transitions are one-way and happen once; after settling it's permanently fulfilled or rejected.

followUps.question: What happens if you call resolve twice?
followUps.answer: Only the first call takes effect; later resolve/reject calls are silently ignored.

theory.question: Compare Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any.
theory.directAnswer: Promise.all waits for ALL to fulfill and returns their values, but rejects immediately on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled waits for all to settle and returns a status object for each, never rejecting. Promise.race settles as soon as the FIRST promise settles, whether it fulfills or rejects. Promise.any fulfills with the first FULFILLMENT and only rejects (with an AggregateError) if every promise rejects.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Four combinators for coordinating multiple promises.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real apps often need to run several async operations together with different success/failure semantics.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: all aggregates values (fail-fast); allSettled aggregates outcomes (never fails); race takes the first to settle; any takes the first to succeed.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right combinator affects latency and resilience and is a very common interview discrimination question.
theory.realWorldExample: Use Promise.all to load a page's required data in parallel; use allSettled for a dashboard where some widgets may fail independently.

nestedTopics.title: Fail-fast vs. resilient
nestedTopics.explanation: all is fail-fast; allSettled tolerates partial failure.

nestedTopics.title: First-settle vs. first-fulfill
nestedTopics.explanation: race reacts to the first settle; any to the first success.

followUps.question: How do you implement a request timeout?
followUps.answer: Promise.race the request against a promise that rejects after N ms — whichever settles first wins.

followUps.question: What does Promise.any reject with?
followUps.answer: An AggregateError whose .errors array holds every individual rejection reason.

scenario.question: A page makes three independent API calls but loads slowly because each await waits for the previous one. How do you fix it, and what changes if one call might fail?
scenario.directAnswer: The calls are independent, so they shouldn't be awaited sequentially. I'd start all three at once and await Promise.all of them, turning total time from the sum of latencies into the max. If one call is allowed to fail without sinking the whole page, I'd switch to Promise.allSettled so the others still resolve and I can handle each failure individually rather than rejecting everything.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Parallelizing independent async work and choosing failure semantics.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Awaiting independent operations one-by-one needlessly serializes latency.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Kick off all promises before awaiting; Promise.all aggregates (fail-fast), allSettled aggregates outcomes (fault-tolerant).

scenario.whyImportant: It's a real performance win and a frequent interview scenario testing both timing and resilience.

nestedTopics.title: Sequential vs. parallel await
nestedTopics.explanation: Awaiting in a loop serializes; starting first then awaiting parallelizes.

nestedTopics.title: Partial failure
nestedTopics.explanation: allSettled lets some calls fail without failing the rest.

followUps.question: Why is `await a(); await b();` slower than Promise.all([a(), b()])?
followUps.answer: The first form starts b only after a resolves; Promise.all starts both immediately, so total time is the slower of the two, not the sum.

coding.question: Implement your own promiseAll(promises): resolve with an array of all values in order, or reject as soon as any input rejects.
coding.thoughtProcess: I return a new Promise. I track results in an array sized to the input and a count of how many have resolved. For each input I use Promise.resolve to normalize non-promises, then on fulfillment store the value at its index and increment the count; when the count equals the length I resolve with the results array. Any rejection rejects the outer promise immediately (fail-fast), and since promises settle once, the first rejection wins.
coding.lineByLine: We create an outer promise. `results` preserves order by index; `remaining` counts pending promises. An empty input resolves immediately. Each input is normalized with Promise.resolve so plain values work too; on fulfillment we store the value at its original index and decrement the counter, resolving once all are done. Passing `reject` as the rejection handler makes the whole thing fail-fast on the first error.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) to register handlers over n promises.

alternativeApproaches.title: allSettled variant
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Never reject; instead store {status, value/reason} per index and resolve when all settle.
alternativeApproaches.code: // on reject: results[i] = { status: 'rejected', reason }; decrement remaining

followUps.question: Why use Promise.resolve(p) inside the loop?
followUps.answer: It normalizes non-promise values (and thenables) into promises so promiseAll works even when the array mixes values and promises.

followUps.question: Why does ordering hold even though promises settle at different times?
followUps.answer: Because each value is written to results[i] by index, not by completion order.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Promises are the async backbone of modern frontends: data layers, caching, and request orchestration are built on promise chains and combinators, with async/await as the ergonomic surface on top.
productionDeepDive.performance: Parallelizing independent requests with Promise.all cuts latency from the sum to the max of operations. Reaction callbacks are microtasks, so long promise chains can still delay rendering if they never yield to a macrotask.
productionDeepDive.security: Always attach a .catch (or try/catch with await) — unhandled rejections can crash Node processes and leak error details; sanitize errors before surfacing them to users or logs.
productionDeepDive.scaling: For large fan-outs, cap concurrency (a promise pool) instead of firing thousands at once; use allSettled so one failure doesn't discard all successful results in resilient batch jobs.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Flat promise chains and async/await read far better than nested callbacks; centralize error handling with a trailing .catch and avoid mixing callback and promise styles in the same flow.
productionDeepDive.observability: Listen for unhandledrejection (browser) / unhandledRejection (Node) to detect missing catches; structured logging in .catch handlers makes async failures traceable.

caseStudies.problem: Sequential awaits made pages load slowly and a single failed request broke the whole view.
caseStudies.solution: Parallelize with Promise.all for required data and Promise.allSettled for independent widgets, with per-call error handling.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more complex coordination for major latency and resilience gains.
caseStudies.lessons: Pick the combinator that matches your latency and failure requirements.

When would you choose allSettled over all?

keyTakeaways: A promise represents an eventual async result and is always pending, fulfilled, or rejected; it settles exactly once and is then immutable.
then/catch/finally each return a new promise, enabling flat chaining where each step's return value feeds the next.
Errors and thrown exceptions skip ahead to the next .catch, giving async code structured, throw/catch-style error propagation.
Use Promise.all (fail-fast parallel), allSettled (resilient), race (first to settle), and any (first to fulfill) to coordinate multiple promises.
Promise reaction callbacks run as microtasks — after synchronous code but before any setTimeout/macrotask.
